stub: {"stubId": "maui-20", "topic": "maui", "slug": "maui-detail-page-never-collected", "level": "senior", "type": "situation", "subtopic": "Lifecycle", "angle": "App memory grows by several megabytes every time a user opens and closes an order detail page. How do you find what keeps the page alive?", "answerHinge": "First prove that the popped page is not collected (a WeakReference check after a forced GC, or dotnet-gcdump from the device). Then trace its root, typically a subscription to a long-lived service or messenger, a singleton-registered page or view model, or a platform cycle in a custom handler.", "sources": ["https://github.com/dotnet/maui/wiki/Memory-Leaks", "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/diagnostics/dotnet-gcdump"]}
Generator notes: Claim that Debug builds with Hot Reload or XAML tooling can keep extra references, so leak checks should be done in Release without the debugger: I believe the dotnet/maui Memory-Leaks wiki says something similar, but the exact wording should be checked.; Claim that dotnet-gcdump on Android and iOS works through dotnet-dsrouter, while on Windows and Mac Catalyst it can attach directly: based on the MAUI wiki and diagnostics docs; build settings needed to enable the diagnostic port are deliberately not named.; Claim about iOS and Mac Catalyst strong reference cycles between NSObject subclasses that the GC cannot break: summarised from the dotnet/maui Memory-Leaks wiki; the precise conditions (C# subclasses of NSObject referencing each other) should be verified.; Claim that WeakEventManager (Microsoft.Maui) is an appropriate weak-event helper for app code: the class exists in MAUI, but whether it is recommended for subscribing to a long-lived service event in app code should be confirmed.; The claim that a debugger or Hot Reload can itself keep objects alive (so leak checks should use a Release build without them) is based on my memory of the dotnet/maui Memory-Leaks wiki; please confirm the wiki says this.; Using dotnet-dsrouter to forward the diagnostics connection for dotnet-gcdump on Android and iOS devices is my understanding of the documented MAUI workflow; please confirm that the wiki or the diagnostics docs describe dsrouter for both platforms.; The statement that dotnet-gcdump triggers a full generation 2 garbage collection before it captures the dump should be checked against the dotnet-gcdump page.; Reference cycles between an NSObject subclass and managed objects on iOS and Mac Catalyst that the GC cannot break: I recall the MAUI Memory-Leaks wiki describing this (along with the MemoryAnalyzers package), but I am not fully sure of the exact conditions it gives.; Application.Current.RequestedThemeChanged is used as an example of a long-lived event source. I believe Application.RequestedThemeChanged exists as an instance event in .NET MAUI; please confirm the name.; I did not state when MAUI calls DisconnectHandler automatically, because that policy may differ between versions (for example a HandlerProperties.DisconnectPolicy setting in later versions). The answer only says that native subscriptions should be removed in DisconnectHandler.

stub: {"stubId": "exceptions-15", "topic": "exceptions", "slug": "release-symbols-line-numbers-in-stack-traces", "level": "lead", "type": "multi", "subtopic": "debugging in production", "angle": "Production stack traces have no file names or line numbers; which build and release practices fix that and keep dumps debuggable?", "answerHinge": "Line numbers appear only when matching PDBs are available at runtime (deployed next to the assembly or embedded with DebugType embedded), and archiving symbols with Source Link lets later dumps map to the exact commit.", "sources": ["https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/compiler-options/code-generation", "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/library-guidance/sourcelink"]}
Generator notes: Claim that the .NET runtime reads embedded portable PDBs (DebugType embedded) when building Exception.StackTrace line info: believed true since .NET Core 2.1, verify.; Claim that in SDK-style projects the Release configuration produces a portable PDB by default and that dotnet publish includes the project's .pdb in the publish output (so loss usually happens in Dockerfile/pipeline copying).; Claim that the runtime/debugger matches PDB to assembly by an identifier in the debug directory (PDB ID), so a PDB from a different build does not fit; deterministic rebuilds were intentionally not discussed.; Claim that the Source Link library guidance page recommends ContinuousIntegrationBuild=true in CI builds; verify the page wording.; Claim in option f explanation that Source Link data lives inside the PDB (not the assembly) and is used by debuggers, not by the runtime for stack traces.; Link https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/diagnostics/symbols was taken from the topic outline (exceptions-17 sources); confirm it exists and covers symbol servers/PDB matching.; Claim that Source Link is included in the .NET SDK and enabled by default since .NET 8 for common Git hosts (GitHub, Azure Repos, GitLab, Bitbucket): believed correct, verify against the Source Link docs or the .NET 8 SDK release notes.; `<DebugType>none</DebugType>` as the MSBuild way to build without symbols: widely used, but the linked code-generation page may list only full/pdbonly/portable/embedded for DebugType. Verify that `none` is a documented value, or replace it with `<DebugSymbols>false</DebugSymbols>`.; Claim that the .NET runtime reads embedded portable PDBs (DebugType embedded), not only side-by-side .pdb files, when it formats Exception.StackTrace with file and line info: believed true since .NET Core 2.1 or later, worth confirming.; The explanation says the Source Link documentation recommends `ContinuousIntegrationBuild` in CI. I believe the library-guidance Source Link page mentions it alongside deterministic builds; confirm the page still contains this recommendation.; Option e: the debugger matches a PDB to an assembly by the PDB identity (ID/signature in the CodeView debug directory entry). A bit-for-bit deterministic rebuild of the exact same commit with the same toolchain could reproduce a matching PDB, but the option says the head of the branch, so it stays incorrect. The fact-checker should confirm that this wording leaves no room for disagreement.
